query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the tribo-corrosion degradation resistance of HEAs alloyed with refractory elements to that of traditional structural alloys in extreme environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs alloyed with refractory elements do not show improved tribo-corrosion degradation resistance compared to traditional structural alloys, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . decision.trend: The trend in the research is to develop high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with superior degradation resistance compared to traditional structural alloys. The studies have explored various processing techniques, such as spark plasma sintering, selective laser melting, and laser cladding, to create HEAs with unique microstructures and properties. The research has also investigated the effects of alloy composition, temperature, and environment on the degradation behavior of HEAs. The findings suggest that HEAs can exhibit improved strength, hardness, and corrosion resistance compared to traditional alloys, making them promising candidates for applications in extreme environments.
decision.unsolved: One of the remaining challenges is to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in HEAs, which are often strong but brittle. Additionally, the degradation mechanisms of HEAs under complex environmental conditions, such as high-temperature and high-pressure conditions, are not yet fully understood. Further research is needed to develop HEAs with balanced properties and to elucidate their degradation behavior under various environmental conditions.
decision.why: The next step in the research is to explore the effect of alloying with refractory elements, such as W, Ta, and Hf, on the degradation resistance of HEAs. These elements have been shown to improve the high-temperature strength and corrosion resistance of HEAs. By introducing these elements into the alloy composition, researchers can develop HEAs with enhanced degradation resistance and balanced properties, making them more suitable for applications in extreme environments.
